<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm1}
Suppose that $h(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$. The zero solution of the linear delay difference equation (\ref{pmap}) is asymptotically stable if $|\lambda| + |\delta| < 1$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Set $q=|\lambda|+|\delta|<1$. Induction gives $|x_n|\leq |x_0|$ for every $n$, so the solution is bounded and the zero solution is stable. Let
\[
L=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|x_n|.
\]
Because $h(n)\to\infty$, we also have $\limsup_{n\to\infty}|x_{h(n)}|\leq L$. Taking the upper limit in
\[
|x_{n+1}|\leq |\lambda|\,|x_n|+|\delta|\,|x_{h(n)}|
\]
therefore yields $L\leq qL$. Since $q<1$, it follows that $L=0$, and hence $x_n\to0$.
\qed
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
The assumption $h(n)\to\infty$ is essential. For example, if $h(n)=0$ and $\delta\ne0$, the persistent term $\delta x_0$ generally prevents convergence to zero. The condition $|\lambda|+|\delta|<1$ is sufficient but not necessary for proportional delays. Figure \ref{fig02} shows a numerically decaying orbit of (\ref{pmap}) with $\lambda=-0.50$, $\delta=0.52$, and $h(n)=\lfloor 0.2n\rfloor$, even though $|\lambda|+|\delta|>1$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm2}
If $\lambda,\delta\geq0$ and $\lambda+\delta>1$, then the zero solution of (\ref{pmap}) is not asymptotically stable for any delay function satisfying $h(n)\leq n$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
Choose $x_0>0$. If $x_j\geq x_0$ for $0\leq j\leq n$, then
\[
x_{n+1}=\lambda x_n+\delta x_{h(n)}\geq(\lambda+\delta)x_0>x_0.
\]
The assertion follows by induction: the solution cannot converge to zero.
\qed
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm5}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{thm2}, if $\lambda>0$, $\delta>0$, and $h$ is monotone non-decreasing, then the solution with $x_0>0$ is strictly increasing.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
Assume $x_0>0$. Since $\lambda>0$ and $\delta>0$, all subsequent iterates are positive.

We show by induction that $\{x_n\}$ is strictly increasing and hence does not converge to zero.

Indeed, since $h(0)=0$,
\begin{equation*}
x_1=\lambda x_0 + \delta x_{h(0)}=  \lambda x_0 + \delta x_0 > x_0.  
\end{equation*}

Assume that $x_n>x_{n-1}$ for $n=1,2,\cdots,k$. Since $h$ is monotone non-decreasing, $h(k)\geq h(k-1)$. Therefore,

\begin{equation*}
    x_{k+1}=\lambda x_k + \delta x_{h(k)} > \lambda x_{k-1} + \delta x_{h(k-1)}=x_k.
\end{equation*}
Thus, $x_n$ is strictly increasing by induction.
\qed
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm3}
If
\[
|\lambda|>1+|\delta|,
\]
then the zero solution of (\ref{pmap}) is unstable for every delay function satisfying $h(n)\leq n$. More precisely, every solution with $x_0\ne0$ is unbounded.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
Set $q=|\lambda|-|\delta|>1$. We prove inductively that
\[
|x_{n+1}|\geq q|x_n|>|x_n|.
\]
Since $h(0)=0$, the reverse triangle inequality gives
\[
|x_1|=|\lambda+\delta|\,|x_0|
\geq (|\lambda|-|\delta|)|x_0|=q|x_0|.
\]
Now suppose that $|x_0|<|x_1|<\cdots<|x_n|$. Because $h(n)\leq n$, we have $|x_{h(n)}|\leq |x_n|$. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
|x_{n+1}|
&=|\lambda x_n+\delta x_{h(n)}|\\
&\geq |\lambda|\,|x_n|-|\delta|\,|x_{h(n)}|\\
&\geq (|\lambda|-|\delta|)|x_n|
=q|x_n|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $|x_n|\geq q^n|x_0|\to\infty$, proving instability.
\qed
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm4}
Let $h(n)=\lfloor an\rfloor$, where $0<a<1$. If
\[
|\delta|>1+|\lambda|,
\]
then the zero solution of (\ref{pmap}) is unstable. More precisely, every solution with $x_0\ne0$ has an unbounded subsequence.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
Set
\[
c=\frac{|\delta|}{1+|\lambda|}>1.
\]
For every integer $k\geq0$, the interval
\[
\left[\frac{k}{a},\frac{k+1}{a}\right)
\]
has length $1/a>1$. It therefore contains an integer $n>k$ satisfying $\lfloor an\rfloor=k$.

Starting with $k_0=0$, suppose that $k_j$ has been chosen, and select $n_j>k_j$ such that $\lfloor an_j\rfloor=k_j$. From (\ref{pmap}),
\[
\delta x_{k_j}=x_{n_j+1}-\lambda x_{n_j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\delta|\,|x_{k_j}|
&\leq |x_{n_j+1}|+|\lambda|\,|x_{n_j}|\\
&\leq(1+|\lambda|)
\max\{|x_{n_j}|,|x_{n_j+1}|\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Choose $k_{j+1}\in\{n_j,n_j+1\}$ so that
\[
|x_{k_{j+1}}|=\max\{|x_{n_j}|,|x_{n_j+1}|\}.
\]
Then $k_{j+1}>k_j$ and
\[
|x_{k_{j+1}}|\geq c|x_{k_j}|.
\]
It follows inductively that
\[
|x_{k_j}|\geq c^j|x_0|\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus the solution has an unbounded subsequence, and the zero solution is unstable.
\qed
<!-- end head-6 -->
